To use creo que / pienso que / me parece que + INDICATIVE (stating an opinion).
To use no creo que / no pienso que / dudo que + SUBJUNCTIVE (expressing doubt).
To express probability: quizás / tal vez + subjunctive or indicative, a lo mejor + indicative.
To use es posible / es probable / puede que + subjunctive.
To discuss and negotiate a holiday plan.
A week after the wedding. Ana and Mihai are planning their honeymoon: Mihai wants to go to Romania, to his grandfather’s village. Ana has… a few doubts.
So, are we going to Romania in July? I think it’s the best time.
Sounds good to me. But I don’t think there’s wifi in your grandfather’s village.
You’re right, there isn’t. But I think it’s good to disconnect for a week.
And is it very cold in the mountains? I read that it snows a lot in the Carpathians.
In July? No, I don’t think it’s cold. It’s warm during the day and cool at night.
OK. And is it true there are bears in the forest?
Yes, there are bears. But I doubt we’ll see one. They’re very shy.
Aunt Pepa says there are vampires in Romania. I don’t think it’s true… or is it?
Ha-ha. Your aunt exaggerates. But maybe my grandfather will tell you the legend of Dracula. He loves scaring tourists.
I’m not a tourist! I’m the new granddaughter.
True. I’m sure he’ll treat you like a queen.
And afterwards? Maybe we could go to the seaside for a few days?
We might go to the Black Sea. It’s likely to be crowded, but it’s gorgeous.
Sounds like a perfect plan to me. Mountains, a grandfather, shy bears, vampires that don’t exist and a beach.
And lots of food. I don’t think you’ll go back to Spain the same weight.
Well, I might change my mind about the trip…
I doubt it. You’ve already tried my mother’s cozonac.
kee-THAS (in Spain z = English “th”) or kee-SAS (Latin America). tal-BES: the “v” is pronounced b.
DOO-do-keh: the d between vowels is very soft, almost like the “th” in English “this”.
“No creo que sea verdad… ¿o sí?” Your voice falls on “verdad”, then rises sharply on “¿o sí?”.
1. Creo que + indicative, no creo que + subjunctive
This is one of the most important rules at B1. When you STATE an opinion, you present it as a fact (for you) → INDICATIVE. When you DENY it, you enter the zone of doubt → SUBJUNCTIVE.
No me parece que tenga razón.
No estoy seguro de que venga.

The classic mistake once you’ve learned the subjunctive: using it everywhere, as in “Creo que sea…”. NO! After affirmative creo que comes the INDICATIVE: Creo que es. And in English “I think it IS” / “I don’t think it IS” use the same verb, so remember: only the negative switches.
A question can take either: ¿Crees que es verdad? (neutral) / ¿Crees que sea verdad? (more doubt, common in Latin America).
2. Doubt: dudo que, no es verdad que
No es verdad que haya vampiros.
No es cierto que nieve en julio.
The opposite is symmetrical: No dudo que tiene razón (I don’t doubt he’s right) → INDICATIVE, because now you’re sure!
3. Maybe: quizás, tal vez, a lo mejor
“A lo mejor” does NOT mean “the best”, it means “maybe”. A lo mejor llueve = Maybe it’ll rain. It’s used all the time in everyday speech in Spain.
If you don’t know which to choose, use “a lo mejor + indicative” or “puede que + subjunctive”. You’ll almost always be right.
This is how you express how sure you are, from 100% to 0%:
A lo mejor viene. / Quizás venga.
See the pattern? As long as you’re fairly sure: indicative. When your certainty drops below half: subjunctive.
5. How to give and ask for an opinion in a discussion
Tienes razón. Estoy de acuerdo. Me parece bien.
No estoy de acuerdo. No creo que sea así. Yo no lo veo así.
He cambiado de opinión. Pensándolo bien…
“¿Qué te parece?” is the Spaniards’ favourite question: ¿Qué te parece si vamos al cine? (How about going to the cinema?).

Ana reads a blog post before the trip. The author answers the mistaken ideas Spaniards have about Romania.
Many Spaniards think Romania is a cold, grey country. I don’t think they know the Romanian summer: in July, in Bucharest, it can reach forty degrees.
Others think Romanian is a Slavic language. It isn’t true that it’s Slavic: it’s a Latin language, like Spanish, Italian or French.
That’s why a Spaniard is very likely to understand words like “casă”, “masă” or “carne” without a translation.
And Dracula? It’s true there was a prince called Vlad, but I doubt he drank blood. Historians say he was cruel, not a vampire.
What is true is that more bears live in the Carpathians than in almost any other country in Europe. But you’re unlikely to see one unless you go into the forest at night.
And a tip: if someone invites you for a meal in a village, don’t say you’re not hungry. Nobody will believe you. And they might serve you three more plates.
¿Qué temperatura puede hacer en Bucarest en julio?
¿Qué tipo de lengua es el rumano?
¿Qué no debes decir si te invitan a comer?
Grandpa Gheorghe’s village was at the end of a narrow road, between green mountains and dark forests. To get there, Ana and Mihai drove four hours from Bucharest.
When the car stopped in front of the house, a very thin man with an old hat and a white moustache was waiting for them at the gate.
“Ana!” he said in Romanian, and gave her three kisses. Then he said something to Mihai and they both laughed.
“What did he say?” asked Ana. “He says you’re prettier than in the video. And that he doesn’t think I deserve you.”
The house was small, made of wood, with flowers in every window. In the yard there were chickens, two sheep and a huge dog called Lup.
Ana didn’t think such a big dog could be so affectionate, but Lup lay down at her feet and didn’t move all afternoon.
That evening they had dinner in the yard, under the stars. Grandpa had made mămăligă, sheep’s cheese and some sausages he had made himself.
Ana ate until she couldn’t eat any more. But Grandpa put another plate in front of her. “It’s impossible for me to be hungry,” Ana thought. And she ate it.
When they had finished, Grandpa lit his pipe and looked towards the forest. A strange silence fell. Even Lup pricked up his ears.
“Now,” Mihai whispered to Ana, “I think the legend is coming.”
Grandpa began to speak slowly. Mihai translated sentence by sentence.
“Many years ago, when I was young, a huge white she-bear lived in this forest. Nobody had ever seen her up close. Some said she didn’t exist. Others, that she was a spirit.”
“One winter night, I got lost in the snow. It was so cold I thought I was going to die. Then I saw two eyes shining among the trees.”
Ana had goosebumps. She didn’t believe in spirits, but in that dark yard, with the forest so close, anything seemed possible.
“It was the white she-bear. She came closer slowly. I was sure she was going to eat me. But she lay down next to me, the way Lup is doing with you now, and kept me warm all night.”
“In the morning, when I woke up, she was gone. There were only tracks in the snow, leading towards the village. I followed them and that’s how I got home.”
“And is it true?” asked Ana, wide-eyed.
Grandpa smiled and said something else. Mihai took a few seconds to translate, because he had got a little emotional.
“He says he’s not sure it was a she-bear. It may have been his imagination, because of the cold. But he says that same spring he met my grandmother.”
“And what does the she-bear have to do with your grandmother?”
Mihai smiled. “My grandmother had very, very white hair. Since she was young. And she was the only person in the village who wasn’t afraid of the forest.”
Ana looked at Grandpa. Grandpa winked at her.
Later, in their room, Ana couldn’t sleep. The smell of the forest came in through the open window.
“Mihai, do you think the story is true?”
“I don’t think there are white she-bears in the Carpathians,” he answered, half asleep. “But I think Grandpa loved my grandmother very much. That part is definitely true.”
Ana lay there thinking. Maybe some stories don’t need to be true to be true.
The next morning, Ana woke up early and went out into the yard. Mist covered the forest. Lup was standing by the gate, looking towards the trees.
And in the mud, by the fence, there were some big, round tracks leading towards the forest.
Ana looked at them for a long time. Then she went back into the house without saying anything. She doubted anyone would believe her.
In the kitchen, Grandpa was already making coffee. He looked at her, saw her face and didn’t ask anything. He just smiled, as if he knew everything.
